cards.statement: Jobs in different projects can reuse a cache by choosing the same `cache:key`.
cards.explanation: GitLab scopes caches to a project. Matching cache keys do not make one project's cache available to another.
cards.misconception: Identical cache keys make caches available across projects.

cards.statement: GitLab separates caches for protected and non-protected branches by default.
cards.explanation: Separate cache keys form a security boundary. A project can change this default behavior.

cards.statement: `cache:key:files` derives the cache key from the contents of the files a job lists.
cards.explanation: GitLab bases this key on listed file contents, so a changed dependency lockfile selects a new cache.

cards.statement: A job with `cache:policy: pull` uploads its changed cache when the job finishes.
cards.explanation: The pull cache policy downloads an existing cache at job startup and skips uploading cache changes.
cards.misconception: The pull policy also publishes changes to the cache.

cards.statement: A job can continue when GitLab Runner misses both the requested cache and its fallback caches.
cards.explanation: A cache miss leaves the job running with no restored cache. The script may need to recreate the missing files.

cards.statement: GitLab Runner restores a job's cache before it downloads the job's artifacts.
cards.explanation: Artifact extraction happens after cache restoration, so an artifact can replace a cached file at the same path.

cards.statement: GitLab Runner uploads a failed job's `artifacts:paths` files by default.
cards.explanation: Ordinary artifact uploads default to on_success. Use artifacts:when to change which job outcomes upload those files.
cards.misconception: Ordinary artifact files upload after failed jobs by default.

cards.statement: GitLab Runner uploads a generated `artifacts:reports` file even when the job's script fails.
cards.explanation: Report artifacts upload for both successful and failed jobs, so GitLab can retain reports from a failed test run.

cards.statement: Jobs in later stages download artifacts from jobs in previous pipeline stages by default.
cards.explanation: GitLab places the earlier jobs' artifacts in the consuming job's working directory.

cards.statement: A job's `dependencies` list supports downloading artifacts from another job in the same stage.
cards.explanation: The dependencies list accepts jobs from earlier stages. Its stage restriction excludes jobs in the consuming job's own stage.
cards.misconception: The dependencies keyword accepts artifact producers in the same stage.

cards.statement: GitLab Runner uploads `artifacts:paths` after a job times out when `artifacts:when` is `always`.
cards.explanation: Setting artifacts:when to always still skips ordinary artifact uploads for jobs that time out.
cards.misconception: The always condition covers artifact uploads after job timeouts.

cards.statement: With latest artifact retention enabled, `artifacts:expire_in` removes the latest successful pipeline's artifacts.
cards.explanation: GitLab keeps artifacts from the most recent successful pipeline for a ref while retention is enabled, despite expire_in.
cards.misconception: An expire_in deadline overrides retention of the latest successful pipeline's artifacts.

cards.statement: GitLab creates a missing environment when a deployment job declares it with `environment`.
cards.explanation: An environment entry in a deployment job creates the named environment if the project does not have it yet.

cards.statement: A deployment job can use a variable exported in `script` to build its `environment:name` value.
cards.explanation: GitLab expands environment:name before the job script runs, so script-created variables are unavailable for that name.
cards.misconception: Variables created by a job script are available when GitLab expands its environment name.

cards.statement: A deployment job puts the shell commands that clean up its environment directly in `environment:on_stop`.
cards.explanation: The on_stop value names a separate stop job; that job's script performs the cleanup.
cards.misconception: The on_stop keyword accepts cleanup commands rather than a job name.

cards.statement: Under the default stopping behavior, GitLab stops an environment when its associated branch is deleted.
cards.explanation: GitLab's default stopping behavior links an environment's lifetime to its associated branch.
cards.volatilityNote: GitLab is reviewing automatic stopping of environments when their associated branch is deleted or merged.

cards.statement: Each deployment resets the environment's expiry period specified by `environment:auto_stop_in`.
cards.explanation: A new deployment starts the configured lifetime again, extending the environment's scheduled stop time.

cards.statement: GitLab creates a deployment record for an environment when a job uses `environment:action: prepare`.
cards.explanation: The prepare environment action accesses the environment for preparation and bypasses deployment creation.
cards.misconception: The prepare action creates a deployment record like the start action.

cards.statement: A job can override GitLab's guessed environment tier with `environment:deployment_tier`.
cards.explanation: GitLab guesses a tier from the environment name unless the job declares a deployment_tier value.

cards.statement: GitLab marks a pipeline as failed while it waits for a blocking manual deployment job.
cards.explanation: A pipeline waiting for a blocking manual job has blocked status. Running the job lets the pipeline continue.
cards.misconception: Waiting for a blocking manual job gives the pipeline a failed status.

cards.statement: GitLab starts the `start_in` timer for a `when: delayed` job when it creates the pipeline.
cards.explanation: A delayed job's timer starts after the previous stage completes successfully.
cards.misconception: A delayed job's waiting period begins at pipeline creation.

cards.statement: `resource_group` makes jobs with the same resource mutually exclusive across pipelines in a project.
cards.explanation: A job waits for another job using its resource group to finish, even when the jobs belong to different pipelines.

cards.statement: Prevent outdated deployment jobs determines deployment job age from the commit timestamp.
cards.explanation: GitLab determines deployment job age from the job's start time rather than the commit time.
cards.misconception: Commit timestamps determine which deployment job is outdated.

cards.statement: In GitLab Premium and Ultimate, Allowed to deploy restricts who starts protected manual deployment jobs.
cards.explanation: A protected environment's Allowed to deploy list controls access to its manual deployment jobs. GitLab administrators also have access.

cards.statement: A matching `merge_request_event` rule in an included file satisfies the merge request pipeline prerequisite.
cards.explanation: Merge request pipelines require a matching job rule or workflow rule directly in `.gitlab-ci.yml`. Included rules do not meet that prerequisite.
cards.misconception: Included rules alone satisfy the merge request pipeline prerequisite.

cards.statement: A merge request pipeline tests the source branch's contents alone.
cards.explanation: GitLab uses the source branch for a merge request pipeline and ignores the target branch's content.

cards.statement: GitLab runs a fork's merge request pipeline in the parent project by default.
cards.explanation: GitLab normally creates and runs a fork's merge request pipeline in the fork project.
cards.misconception: Fork merge request pipelines run in the parent project by default.

cards.statement: For a fork merge request pipeline run in the parent project, GitLab reads the parent's branch configuration.
cards.explanation: A fork's merge request pipeline run in the parent project uses the CI/CD configuration from the fork's branch.
cards.misconception: Running a fork pipeline in the parent project switches its configuration to the parent's branch.

cards.statement: GitLab asks users to accept a warning before starting a fork merge request pipeline in the parent project's UI.
cards.explanation: The UI requires the parent project member to accept a warning before starting a pipeline for a fork's merge request.

cards.statement: With merged results pipelines in GitLab Premium and Ultimate, branch conflicts make GitLab run a merge request pipeline.
cards.explanation: Conflicting source and target changes prevent a temporary merged result, so GitLab runs a standard merge request pipeline instead.

cards.statement: In GitLab Premium and Ultimate, a Maintainer can enable merged results pipelines.
cards.explanation: Enabling merged results pipelines requires the Maintainer or Owner role in the project.

cards.statement: In GitLab Premium and Ultimate, merge trains support projects with merged results pipelines turned off.
cards.explanation: GitLab requires merged results pipelines to be enabled before a project uses merge trains.
cards.misconception: Merge trains work independently of the merged results pipelines setting.

cards.statement: In GitLab Premium and Ultimate, a merge train pipeline includes every preceding merge request's changes in that train.
cards.explanation: GitLab combines a queued merge request's changes with those ahead of it to test compatibility with the earlier changes.

cards.statement: In GitLab Premium and Ultimate, merge train pipelines use sequential execution by default.
cards.explanation: GitLab runs merge train pipelines in parallel when capacity is available.
cards.misconception: The train's queue forces its pipelines to execute sequentially.

cards.statement: In GitLab Premium and Ultimate, GitLab keeps a merge request on its train after that request's train pipeline fails.
cards.explanation: GitLab removes a merge request from its train when that merge request's train pipeline fails.
cards.misconception: A failed train pipeline leaves its merge request waiting in the queue.

cards.statement: In GitLab Premium and Ultimate, `rules:changes:compare_to` can match target-branch changes in merged results pipelines.
cards.explanation: The temporary merged commit includes target-branch changes. These can make rules:changes:compare_to match more than the merge request's own changes.

cards.statement: A trigger job can reserve a runner slot while GitLab creates its downstream pipeline.
cards.explanation: GitLab creates downstream pipelines itself; trigger jobs use no runner.
cards.misconception: Trigger jobs occupy runners while creating downstream pipelines.

cards.statement: A trigger job succeeds by default as soon as GitLab creates its downstream pipeline.
cards.explanation: The default trigger status records successful pipeline creation rather than the result of the downstream jobs.

cards.statement: Since GitLab 18.2, each `trigger:strategy: mirror` job matches its downstream pipeline's status.
cards.explanation: A trigger job using mirror tracks the downstream pipeline's status through completion.

cards.statement: A nested trigger job reuses upstream `trigger:forward` settings for received pipeline variables by default.
cards.explanation: Each nested trigger job controls its own forwarding with trigger:forward; the upstream trigger's setting does not propagate.
cards.misconception: An upstream trigger's forwarding configuration automatically carries through later trigger jobs.

cards.statement: A child pipeline runs against the same commit SHA as the parent pipeline that creates it.
cards.explanation: A child pipeline uses the parent's project, ref and commit, so a later branch update does not change its checkout.

cards.statement: GitLab can auto-cancel interruptible child pipelines when a new commit gets a pipeline on the same ref.
cards.explanation: Child pipelines participate in redundant-pipeline auto-cancellation when their jobs are configured to permit interruption.

cards.statement: A multi-project trigger uses the upstream branch name as its downstream branch by default.
cards.explanation: GitLab selects the downstream project's default branch unless the trigger job sets trigger:branch.
cards.misconception: Multi-project triggers reuse the upstream branch name as their downstream default.

cards.statement: The user triggering a multi-project pipeline requires permission to run pipelines in the downstream project.
cards.explanation: GitLab checks the initiating user's access to the downstream project before creating that project's pipeline.

cards.statement: A child of a merge request pipeline has `CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE` set to `merge_request_event`.
cards.explanation: GitLab sets CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE to parent_pipeline in a child pipeline, including one whose parent is a merge request pipeline.
cards.misconception: Child pipelines inherit their merge request parent's CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE value.

cards.statement: A trigger job can read its child pipeline configuration from a YAML file saved as a job artifact.
cards.explanation: trigger:include identifies the generated YAML with artifact and its producing job with job.

cards.statement: Trigger jobs forward pipeline variables to their downstream pipelines by default.
cards.explanation: By default, trigger jobs keep pipeline variables upstream. Set pipeline_variables: true under trigger:forward to pass them.
cards.misconception: Trigger jobs forward runtime pipeline variables by default.

cards.statement: In GitLab Premium and Ultimate, `needs:pipeline:job` can fetch artifacts from an unrelated project's pipeline.
cards.explanation: needs:pipeline:job fetches artifacts from a successful job within the same parent-child pipeline hierarchy.
cards.misconception: needs:pipeline:job can download artifacts from arbitrary projects.
